name: Terneuzen
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement Terneuzen | Chemical Tankers
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Terneuzen for gas carriers, chemical tankers and fertiliser bulkers: ballast tank, hold, deck and cargo piping UTM.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Gas Carriers, Chemical Tankers and Bulkers at Terneuzen
intro: Terneuzen guards the entrance to the Ghent–Terneuzen canal and is where the chemical industry on the Dutch side of North Sea Port is concentrated. Gas carriers and chemical tankers serve the Dow complex, ammonia and fertiliser ships use Yara's plant at Sluiskil, and bulk carriers work the canal-side quays and the outer harbours. Ships here usually stay for a full cargo operation, which makes a measured scope realistic. A technician team flies in from India for each Terneuzen job and joins the vessel at its berth.
keywords: chemical tanker gauging north sea port

highlights.p: LPG, ethylene and ammonia carriers bringing feedstock to the canal zone can be gauged in ballast tanks, double bottom and deck structure while the cargo system stays sealed. Hold spaces around independent cargo tanks need gas-freeing first, so they are planned as a separate job.

Parcel tankers moving between the chemical jetties and the tank terminals often have a quiet spell between discharge and loading. Cargo and ballast piping, pump-room lines and deck structure can be measured then, with the cargo tanks themselves left for a gas-free stop.

Urea, ammonium nitrate and similar cargoes attack hold steel once moisture gets in. Bulk carriers arriving to load at the canal-side berths, holds swept and empty, give a clear look at hold frames, lower brackets and tank tops before the next cargo goes in.

port.h: Terneuzen: lock port, chemical cluster and canal gateway
p: Terneuzen stands on the south bank of the Westerschelde in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen, the strip of Dutch territory between the estuary and the Belgian border. The town grew around the sea locks that lead into the Ghent–Terneuzen canal, and every seagoing ship bound for Ghent passes through them. The lock complex has been enlarged with a new sea lock, the biggest in the complex, built so that larger ships can reach the canal zone and Ghent. Ships come up the Westerschelde under Scheldt pilotage, sharing the fairway with traffic heading on to Antwerp, and those that miss their lock slot wait at anchorage areas in the estuary. Outside the locks, harbours on the estuary side serve ships that never enter the canal at all, and these have their own rhythm of short industrial calls.

The canal zone running south from Terneuzen through Sluiskil and Sas van Gent towards the border forms one continuous industrial corridor. Dow's Terneuzen complex, one of the company's largest production sites, takes in feedstock and ships out chemicals and polymers, so gas carriers, chemical tankers and product tankers make up much of the deep-water traffic. Yara's plant at Sluiskil turns natural gas into ammonia and nitrogen fertilisers, adding ammonia carriers and bulk carriers that load finished product. Dry bulk, agribulk and project cargo use other quays, and inland barges fill the canal between the seagoing calls. The fleet is therefore mostly handysize and medium-range tonnage, and many of those ships are specialised vessels whose cargo systems shape what can be inspected and when.

The tidal range on the Westerschelde is large, and deep-draught ships time the estuary passage to the tide, while the canal behind the locks is held at a steady level. For gauging that matters in two ways. A ship in an estuary-side harbour rises and falls alongside, which affects gangways and the reach of any staging rigged over the side; a ship inside the canal lies at a constant level and is easier to work from the quay. Winter weather on the estuary can stop launch transfers to anchored ships for days at a time, whereas canal berths are sheltered. Lock maintenance and heavy traffic sometimes delay passages, and the agent's lock-slot forecast is the figure around which the team's travel is built.

facilities.h: Where gauging happens around Terneuzen's locks and canal zone
p: Terneuzen is not a docking port for seagoing ships. Vessels that need a drydock go across the estuary to Vlissingen-Oost or to yards further afield, and the Terneuzen call is used to gather the readings that size the steel work before they go. The practical settings are the chemical and gas jetties, the canal-side quays at Sluiskil and beyond, and the outer harbours on the estuary. At the chemical jetties every activity on deck is governed by the terminal's safety rules, and ignition sources are tightly controlled. Battery-powered gauges still count as electrical equipment in a hazardous zone, so each terminal decides what may be used where, and the equipment list goes to the agent well before the ship berths.

Inside the canal, ships loading fertiliser or discharging bulk lie at quays where the main constraint is the cargo plan rather than gas safety. Holds can be gauged once swept, and ballast tanks once the crew has emptied and ventilated them, which suits a team working steadily through the day while cargo continues at other hatches. Ships idle between fixtures, or waiting for an outbound lock slot, sometimes lie at lay-by berths in the canal or the outer harbours, and these are the best places for a longer pre-purchase or owner's condition survey. When a Terneuzen tanker, a Vlissingen docking and a Ghent bulker fall in the same fortnight, the team can be routed through all three without returning home.
list: Chemical and gas jetties serving the Dow complex — deck structure, piping and ballast tank gauging under the terminal's permit; cargo tanks and hold spaces only once gas-free.
Ammonia and fertiliser berths at Sluiskil — hold, hatch coaming and tank-top gauging on bulk carriers before loading, and ballast tank work on ammonia carriers.
Canal-side dry bulk and project cargo quays — hold frame, bracket and hatch cover readings once grabs or cranes have finished.
Outer harbours on the Westerschelde side of the locks — piping, deck and tank gauging on ships that call without entering the canal.
Lay-by berths in the canal zone — longer owner's condition, pre-purchase and on-hire surveys on ships waiting between cargoes.
Westerschelde anchorages — a limited, weather-dependent scope by launch for ships waiting for a lock slot or the tide.

context.h: Inspectors, chemical cargoes and climate rules at Terneuzen
p: Port state control at Terneuzen follows the Paris MoU and is carried out by the Inspectie Leefomgeving en Transport (ILT). Gas carriers and chemical tankers trading here also face the heaviest commercial scrutiny in shipping: vetting under the SIRE and CDI inspection schemes looks at ballast tank coatings, structural condition and piping, and an inspector who finds wastage or a weeping pipe will record it. Owners who gauge ahead of a vetting date, and repair what the readings show, arrive with answers rather than explanations, and the observation never reaches the report.

The EU rules that bind every ship calling at an EU port weigh on this fleet too. Ships of any flag need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and larger ships report emissions under the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime. The canal zone is also preparing for a different industrial future, with low-carbon ammonia, hydrogen and carbon capture projects under discussion around the chemical and fertiliser plants. For owners of ageing ammonia and gas carriers, that adds weight to the question of whether a double hull has the margin for another survey cycle, and thickness data answers it in steel rather than in estimates.

jobs.h: Thickness gauging jobs typical of a Terneuzen call
jobs.p: Terneuzen jobs are shaped by the cargo system on board. On gas carriers and chemical tankers, the line between what can be gauged during a call and what has to wait for gas-freeing is drawn before the team leaves India, so nobody arrives expecting to enter a space that will not be released. On bulk carriers in the canal the limits are time and access in the holds. Most superintendents use a Terneuzen call either to answer a specific question, such as a vetting observation or a suspect pipe, or to build a steel estimate for a docking across the estuary. These are typical scopes:
list: An LPG carrier discharging feedstock at a chemical jetty: ballast tank and double-bottom gauging, plus deck structure readings, while the cargo tanks remain in service.
A chemical parcel tanker between cargoes: wall-thickness readings on ballast and cargo piping in the pump room and on deck, with tank gauging deferred to a gas-free stop.
A handysize bulk carrier loading fertiliser at Sluiskil: hold frames, lower brackets and tank top gauged before loading, ahead of an intermediate survey.
An ammonia carrier facing a vetting inspection: ballast tank structure and areas of coating breakdown gauged, with pitting depths recorded for the superintendent.
Pre-docking gauging on a product tanker in an outer harbour, producing the steel list that travels with the ship to Vlissingen-Oost.

logistics: Brussels Airport and Amsterdam Schiphol both serve Terneuzen; from Brussels the road runs past Ghent to the border, and on the Dutch side the Westerschelde tunnel links Terneuzen with Zuid-Beveland. Chemical sites in the canal zone run their own safety inductions on top of ISPS gate control, so the ship's agent passes the team's names and certificates to the terminal in good time. Technicians coming from India need Schengen visas, which we apply for as soon as the call window is known, and travel is tied to the agent's lock-slot forecast.
vessels: General cargo and project cargo ships

faqs.q: Can cargo tanks on a gas carrier be gauged while it is alongside in Terneuzen?
faqs.a: No. The cargo containment on an LPG, ethylene or ammonia carrier stays in service at the jetty, and the hold spaces around independent tanks are inerted or filled with dry air. What a Terneuzen call allows is the hull outside that system: ballast tanks, double bottom, deck structure, voids that can be ventilated and machinery-space piping. Hold-space and containment work belongs to a docking or a planned gas-freeing.

faqs.q: Do the Terneuzen locks affect when the team can board?
faqs.a: For ships calling inside the canal, yes. Arrival depends on a lock slot, and lock maintenance or a busy period can move it by hours. Once the ship is alongside in the canal zone, the cargo operation decides the working window. For ships in the outer harbours the locks play no part, but the Westerschelde tide affects gangway access and any launch work.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Terneuzen?
faqs.a: Not one that seagoing ships use for dockings; those are taken across the Westerschelde to Vlissingen-Oost or to yards elsewhere in North West Europe. Terneuzen is the place to measure before the docking, so the yard receives a steel estimate based on readings. Where the owner wants it, the same team can carry the measurement programme through at the docking yard.

faqs.q: What corrosion do fertiliser cargoes cause in bulk carrier holds?
faqs.a: Many fertilisers absorb moisture, and once damp they become aggressive to bare steel, attacking hold frames, the lower parts of bulkheads and the tank top where residues collect. Grab damage strips coating and lets the attack start. Gauging at those locations, with pitting depths recorded, tells the owner whether frames and brackets are approaching their allowable diminution before the surveyor makes the same discovery.

faqs.q: Can ultrasonic gauges be used in a terminal's hazardous zone?
faqs.a: Only if the terminal permits it. A battery-powered gauge is still electrical equipment, and some terminals ask for intrinsically safe instruments or a gas test before work starts on deck. We send the equipment list and planned work areas to the agent, the terminal decides, and anything it will not allow is moved to a time when the ship is outside the zone or gas-free.
